title: A delayed project
lines: I've been going through the schedule, and frankly, I don't see how we can hit the March deadline.
I had a feeling you'd say that. Is it the supplier again?

So what are our options? I'd rather not go back to the client empty-handed.
We could run some of the tests in parallel instead of one after another. It's riskier, but it might save us three weeks.
And the rest of the delay?
Honestly, we'd need to bring in two more technicians, at least temporarily. Otherwise we're just hoping for the best.
Right. Put the numbers together, and I'll make the case to management. But I want a realistic date this time, not an optimistic one.

title: After the failure
lines: So, the report's finally in. It turns out the weld didn't fail because of the load at all.
Really? Everyone was so sure we'd miscalculated the stresses.
That was the convenient explanation. In fact, the root cause was fatigue. Tiny cracks had been spreading for months, and nobody picked them up, because the inspections were purely visual.
So, strictly speaking, the design was sound, and it was the maintenance regime that let us down.
Well, I wouldn't let the design off the hook entirely. Had we specified a smoother transition at the joint, the cracks might never have started in the first place.
Fair point. What worries me is that there are a dozen identical structures out there, presumably in the same state.
Exactly. I'm recommending ultrasonic testing on all of them within the month, whatever the cost. The alternative doesn't bear thinking about.
I'll back you on that. It's a hard sell, but nowhere near as hard as explaining a second failure.

q.q: What was the real cause of the failure, and why was it not detected?
q.a: Fatigue: tiny cracks had been spreading for months and went unnoticed because inspections were only visual.

q.a: No. He says a smoother transition at the joint might have prevented the cracks from starting, so the design shares some responsibility.

q.a: Ultrasonic testing of all twelve identical structures within the month; it is expensive, but far less costly than explaining a second failure.

title: No power in the kitchen
lines: Good morning. You called about a problem with the electricity?
Yes, thank you for coming. There is no power in the kitchen. The lights don't work and the fridge is off.

title: The substation upgrade
lines: Thanks for joining the call. I wanted to go over the protection settings before we energise the new transformer.
Good idea. I looked at your study last night. The short-circuit levels are higher than I expected.
They are. Adding the second transformer almost doubles the fault current on the low-voltage side, which means some of the existing breakers are no longer adequate.
How many are we talking about?
Four out of the twelve feeders. Their breaking capacity is twenty-five kiloamps, and we'd be looking at thirty-one in the worst case.
That's not something we can ignore. Could we operate with the bus coupler open, so the transformers never run in parallel?
We could, as a temporary measure. It keeps the fault level down, but we lose the redundancy we were paying for.
Then let's do that for now and order the new breakers. I'd rather lose redundancy for two months than rely on equipment that might not clear a fault.

q.a: It almost doubles the fault current on the low-voltage side, so some existing breakers are no longer adequate.

q.a: Four of the twelve feeders: their breakers are rated at 25 kiloamps and the worst-case fault would be 31.

title: The grid of the future
lines: You've argued that our grids were designed for a world that no longer exists. What exactly do you mean by that?
Well, for a century, the logic was simple: a handful of enormous power stations pushed energy outwards, in one direction, to passive consumers. That assumption is now collapsing.
Solar, batteries, electric cars, you name it. Power now flows both ways, and the old protection schemes, which took the direction of the current for granted, can be fooled.
Some would say the answer is simply to build more lines.

That's the brute-force approach, and it's ruinously expensive. A smarter option is flexibility: paying people to shift their consumption, so that demand follows generation rather than the other way round.
Isn't there a risk that we're making the system too complex to control?
Undoubtedly. But the alternative, clinging to a model built for coal, would be far more dangerous in the long run.

q.a: That a few huge power stations sent energy in one direction to passive consumers.

q.q: What alternative to building more lines does she defend, and what risk does she accept?
q.a: Flexibility: paying people to shift consumption so demand follows generation. She accepts that the system becomes more complex, but says keeping the old model would be more dangerous.

title: The job interview

Have you had any experience managing people?
Not officially, but last year I trained three new colleagues, and I organised the weekly schedule when my supervisor was away.
That's useful. And what would you say is your biggest weakness?
I sometimes find it hard to delegate. I tend to do things myself to make sure they're done properly, but I'm learning to trust other people more.

title: Asking for a raise
lines: Thanks for making time, Helen. I'll get straight to the point: I'd like to discuss my salary.
I thought that might be it. Go ahead.
Over the past year I've taken on the whole northern region, on top of my existing accounts. My targets went up by forty percent, and I exceeded them. My pay, however, hasn't moved.
Nobody's questioning your performance. The trouble is, budgets were frozen in January, and my hands are somewhat tied.
I understand the constraints. But I've had an approach from another firm, and while I'd much rather stay, I can't ignore the difference indefinitely.
I see. I can't promise a number today. What I can do is take this to the director this week and push for an exception.
That's all I'm asking. And if a raise is off the table, I'd be open to other arrangements, such as extra leave or a clearer path to promotion.
That gives me something to work with. Let's speak again on Monday.

title: Restructuring
lines: I gather the announcement didn't go down particularly well on your floor.
That's putting it mildly. People heard the word restructuring and stopped listening. As far as they're concerned, it's redundancies dressed up in corporate language.
Which is ironic, given that no one is actually losing their job.
You and I know that. But the message was buried under so much jargon that it might as well have been written to cause panic.
So what would you have done differently?
Led with the one thing people care about: your job is safe. Then explained what changes, and only then why. Instead, we opened with market headwinds and synergies.
Point taken. Would it help if the director met the teams in person?
It would, provided she's prepared to take awkward questions rather than read from a script. Otherwise it'll only make matters worse.

title: City or countryside
lines: So you're really going through with it? Leaving the city for good?

That's what I thought at first. Then I realised how little of it I actually use. I haven't been to the theatre in two years, yet I pay a fortune to live near one.
I only need to be in the office twice a week now, which changes everything. The commute would have been unbearable five days a week.

title: Always connected
lines: I read your piece on switching off. You seem to think we've sleepwalked into something.
I do. Nobody ever sat down and decided to be reachable sixteen hours a day. It crept up on us, one notification at a time.
Yet most people would say their phone makes life easier.

In countless small ways, it does. But convenience has a cost that's harder to measure. We've lost the ability to be bored, and boredom, oddly enough, is where a good deal of our thinking used to happen.
So what's the remedy? Throwing the phone in a drawer?
Nothing so dramatic. I'm wary of solutions that rely on willpower alone, since the apps are engineered to defeat it. Small barriers work better: no phone in the bedroom, no notifications after eight.
And does it work for you?
Most of the time. I still slip, but at least now I notice when I do, and that's half the battle.

title: The secret of good bread
lines: People assume baking bread is complicated, but there are really only four ingredients: flour, water, salt and time.
Time being the one everybody tries to skip.
Precisely. A slow fermentation, ideally overnight in the fridge, is what develops the flavour. If you rush it with extra yeast, the loaf rises, but it tastes of very little.
My loaves always come out dense. What am I doing wrong?
Most likely the dough is too dry, or you're not letting it rest long enough. A wetter dough is harder to handle, but it gives you those big, open holes.
And the crust? Mine never gets that deep colour.
That's down to steam. Professional ovens inject it; at home, you can bake inside a heavy pot with the lid on for the first twenty minutes.
So the pot traps the moisture from the dough itself. That's rather clever.

q.q: According to the baker, what is the most neglected ingredient and why does it matter?
q.a: Time: a slow fermentation, ideally overnight in the fridge, develops the flavour, while rushing it with extra yeast gives a loaf that tastes of little.

q.q: How can you get a good crust at home?
q.a: By baking inside a heavy pot with the lid on for the first twenty minutes, so it traps the steam from the dough.

title: Tradition on a plate
lines: Your restaurant has been accused of betraying traditional cuisine. Does that criticism sting?

It used to. Now I find it slightly absurd. The dishes people defend as timeless were, more often than not, invented a couple of generations ago, with ingredients that had arrived from the other side of the world.
Not a myth, but a moving target. Tomatoes were once a suspicious novelty in Europe. Cooking has always evolved by borrowing, and to freeze it at an arbitrary date is nostalgia, not respect.
Yet surely something is lost when a grandmother's recipe gets deconstructed into foam.
Absolutely, when it's done for show. Technique for its own sake is as empty as tradition for its own sake. The test is brutally simple: is the dish more delicious, or merely more clever?
And how often do you fail that test?
More often than I'd care to admit. But the failures never reach the menu.

title: Money in football
lines: Another transfer record broken this summer. A hundred and eighty million for one player. Has the game lost its mind?
It certainly looks that way, though the clubs would argue it's just the market. Television money keeps rising, and it has to go somewhere.
It goes to a tiny group of clubs, which is precisely the problem. The same four or five teams win everything, and the rest are there to make up the numbers.
Financial rules were supposed to prevent that.
In theory. In practice, the richest clubs can afford the best lawyers, so the rules bite everyone except the ones they were aimed at.
Would a salary cap work, like in American sports?
It might, but only if every major league adopted it at once. Otherwise the top players would simply move wherever there's no cap.
So we're stuck. Still, people keep watching.
They do, for now. But a competition where the outcome is predictable won't hold its audience forever.

q.q: Where does the money come from and what problem does its distribution create?
q.a: From rising television money, which goes to a tiny group of clubs, so the same four or five teams win everything.

q.q: Why have financial rules failed, according to the man?
q.a: Because the richest clubs can afford the best lawyers, so the rules affect everyone except the clubs they were aimed at.

q.q: What is the weakness of a salary cap?
q.a: It would only work if every major league adopted it at the same time; otherwise top players would move to leagues without a cap.

title: The decline of the number ten
lines: You've written that the classic playmaker, the number ten, is all but extinct. Isn't that a little melodramatic?
Perhaps, but look at the evidence. The modern game leaves no room for a player who strolls around waiting for inspiration. Pressing systems demand that all eleven work without the ball.
So the artists have been sacrificed for athletes.
Not sacrificed, so much as relocated. The creativity is still there; it has simply moved deeper, to midfielders who dictate play from in front of the defence, or wider, to forwards who cut inside.
As a romantic, yes. There was something gloriously inefficient about a player who did nothing for eighty minutes and then won the match with a single pass.
As an analyst, I have to concede that today's teams are better in almost every measurable respect. Whether they're more beautiful to watch is another matter entirely.

q.q: Why has the traditional number ten disappeared, according to the writer?
q.a: Because modern pressing systems require all eleven players to work without the ball, leaving no room for a player who waits for inspiration.

q.q: Where has the creativity gone?
q.a: It has moved deeper, to midfielders who dictate play in front of the defence, or wider, to forwards who cut inside.

q.a: As a romantic he misses the gloriously inefficient genius who decided a match with one pass; as an analyst he admits modern teams are better in almost every measurable way, though not necessarily more beautiful.
